title: Food Blog Newsletter: Substack vs beehiiv vs Kit
summary: Start a food blog newsletter: why an email list protects creators, Substack vs beehiiv vs Kit fees, what to send weekly, and how to grow it from Instagram.
body_markdown:
A food blog newsletter is the most reliable channel most food creators aren't using. You can have a big Instagram following and still lose half your reach overnight when the app changes what it shows.


Our point of view: start the list before you think you need it. Every recipe post that goes out without a sign-up link is a reader you might not reach again. The platform matters less than starting.


## Why a food blog newsletter protects food creators


An email list is the one audience no app controls. Social posts reach whoever the algorithm chooses. An email reaches every subscriber's inbox.


That matters for income too. A weekly send brings readers back to your recipe pages, which lifts ad earnings and grocery commissions. It also gives you something brands value: an audience you can reach on a set date.


## Substack vs beehiiv vs Kit


All three can run a free food newsletter. They differ most in what they charge when you add paid subscriptions.


Platform


Free to start


Cut of paid subscriptions


Worth knowing


Substack


Yes, at any list size


10%, plus Stripe fees


Built-in reader network and app


beehiiv


Yes, up to 2,500 subscribers


0% on paid plans, plus Stripe fees


Paid tiers need a paid plan


Kit


Check current plans


3.5% plus 30 cents per transaction


Strong automations and digital product sales


Sources:


[Substack's pricing help page](https://support.substack.com/hc/en-us/articles/360037607131-How-much-does-Substack-cost)


,


[beehiiv pricing](https://www.beehiiv.com/pricing)


and


[Kit pricing](https://kit.com/pricing)


. Substack lists Stripe card processing at 2.9% plus 30 cents per payment for US cards. Prices change, so check each page before you choose.


A simple rule: Substack is the easiest start, beehiiv suits a growing paid list, and Kit suits creators who sell digital products like meal plans or ebooks.


## What should you send each week?


Keep the format simple enough to repeat. A long magazine-style email is hard to keep up, and a skipped week costs more than a short one.


A weekly format that works:


1.


**One new recipe.**


A photo, two lines on why it's good, and a link to the full recipe page.


2.


**One tip.**


A technique, a swap or a shortcut that took you years to learn.


3.


**One thing from the archive.**


A seasonal recipe readers may have missed.


4.


**One personal line.**


What you're cooking this week, so it reads like a person.


Always link to the recipe page rather than putting the full recipe in the email. The page is where ads, ratings and shoppable ingredients live.

## How do you make money from a recipe newsletter?


Newsletter income for food creators comes from four places:


-


**Traffic to recipe pages.**


Each click earns through ads and grocery commissions on the site.


-


**Paid tiers.**


Members-only recipes, meal plans or early access.


-


**Sponsorships.**


A brand pays for a feature in one send.


-


**Affiliate links.**


Kitchen gear and pantry items you use.


Start free. Add a paid tier once you can see which emails readers open and click most, since that tells you what they'd pay for. Our guide to


[how food bloggers make money](https://www.jupiter.co/blog/how-food-bloggers-make-money)


covers how these streams fit together.


## Growing your list from Instagram


Most food creators' future subscribers already follow them on Instagram. The job is giving them a reason to sign up.


-


Offer a specific freebie, such as a printable weekly meal plan or a holiday baking collection.


-


Mention it in captions and Stories, not just in your bio.


-


Use comment-to-DM automation so followers who comment a keyword get the sign-up link straight away.
